title: Only the Sith Deal in Absolutes
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Using Obi-Wan Kenobi's line from Star Wars Episode III, Stuart Jr. argues against absolutist thinking about students and colleagues. When teachers label students as 'just not AP material' or 'lazy,' or dismiss administrators wholesale, they commit the Sith error of flattening complex human beings into fixed caricatures. The article offers concrete revised formulations for each dismissive label — behavioral observations, curiosity-driven hypotheses, and specific intervention strategies — modeling the nuanced, provisional thinking Stuart calls the Jedi side of teaching. The piece is deliberately playful in tone but serious in its underlying claim that reductive thinking about students and colleagues blocks the relational breakthroughs effective teaching requires.
points: Absolutist student labels exceed what reality supports and block teachers from seeing the specific, addressable behaviors that actually need attention.
Every dismissive label has a behaviorally precise reframing available — one that names the observable problem, opens hypotheses about causes, and points toward a specific intervention.
The 'dark side of the force' in teaching is reducing people to their presenting problems and making those problems the totality of who they are in the teacher's perception.
Treating administrator decisions as evidence of irredeemably bad administrators is the same absolutist error applied to adult colleagues, and it carries the same costs.
The Star Wars frame works pedagogically because it signals the absurdity of absolute thinking while making a genuine claim about the relational damage absolutism does in classrooms.
quotes: Anakin: If you're not with me, then you're my enemy. Obi Wan: Only a Sith deals in absolutes. I will do what I must.
My point is that I often think about this line when I encounter the following kinds of beliefs about students: 'He's just not AP material.' 'She's a terrible student.' 'That kid is lazy.'

He's not studying or asking questions or engaging in class activities. I need to have a conversation with him about the specific concerns I'm having and see what his thoughts are about the AP course he's signed up for.

In teaching and life, the 'dark side of the force' tends to look like reducing people down into caricatures. We take the problems folks present us with and make it the totality of who they are in our hearts.

I'm not seeing much effort out of ol' Johnny. Let's see what might be going on here. It could be something physiological (e.g., lack of sleep) or volitional (e.g., perhaps he thinks school is pointless, in which case I can target the Value belief).
